title: Opinion: France has more to repair than broken windows
seoTitle: France’s unrest: borrowing costs, budgets and public trust
summary: France needs to reassure lenders without dismissing failures in public services. Fiscal credibility requires funded choices and results people can actually see, not just a market-friendly promise.
excerpt: A small yield movement can mean millions on a new loan. But winning back lenders is only part of rebuilding trust in the state.

body:
After last weekend’s looting, damaged shops need to reopen and streets need clearing. Those responsible for destruction should be held accountable. But France has another repair job: convincing both its citizens and its lenders that the state can deliver what it promises.

It will not get there by dismissing every complaint about a school building as unaffordable. Nor by promising more money after every demonstration without explaining where it comes from. France needs a budget that adds up and produces results its citizens can recognise. Pleasing the bond market is not, on its own, a programme for government.

A protester is not automatically a looter

The City of Paris confirms serious damage and looting in several districts. That deserves no minimising.

Nor should a pupil missing a teacher be merged into the same picture as someone emptying a shop. This month the education minister discussed replacements, buildings and the school day with pupils. These are matters on which a government should answer questions. Violence does not resolve them; treating every grievance as violence does not resolve them either.

The immediate bill also falls on different balance sheets. A trader, an insurer and a local authority may bear different parts of it. There is no verified total here that can simply be entered as an exact addition to the French public deficit.

On Monday, borrowing became more expensive too

The financial response deserves the same precision. The ten-year yield index published by the Banque de France rose from 4.794% on Friday 16 October to 4.853% on Monday 19 October. That is 0.059 percentage point, or 5.9 basis points. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point.

Reuters described a sell-off in French bonds that Monday and investor concerns about the government’s political ability to carry out fiscal adjustment. This supports a plausible connection between instability and funding. It does not isolate the share of every extra fraction of interest caused by the riots. Inflation expectations and broader market movements matter too.

For a fixed-rate bond, price and market yield generally move in opposite directions. The concern is therefore not that French bonds are rising in price, but that lenders demand a higher return for new financing.

What do those hundredths mean in euros?

Take a fictional new €10 billion loan with a ten-year maturity. Assume it is funded entirely at the higher rate, issued at par, with the same principal and no fees. The difference gives this approximation:

€10 billion × 0.00059 = about €5.9 million extra per full year.

That makes a small percentage tangible. It is emphatically not a bill France has demonstrably received because of the weekend. To establish that, we would need its actual borrowing amounts, maturities and terms. The premium could fall again. We therefore apply it neither to all outstanding French debt nor automatically to ten years.

Existing fixed-rate borrowing does not all become more expensive on Monday morning. Pressure builds gradually through new loans and refinancing debt that matures. Our comparison of annual government interest costs shows a different measure: a yearly budget expense, not today’s market yield.

High spending does not guarantee a lesson is taught

The other easy story is that France has run out of money. It can still borrow: the debt agency allocated €7.245 billion in short-term bills on 19 October. That establishes access to that market, not an unlimited ability to afford new spending.

Insee’s provisional accounts put public spending at 57.3% of gross domestic product in 2025. That is not an education budget. It includes pensions, healthcare and social benefits, among other items. A large national total does not prove that every school has the teachers it needs.

There are nevertheless grounds to ask what the money delivers. In December 2025, France’s public auditor found that 9% of compulsory teaching hours had not been delivered in public collèges, lower-secondary schools, in 2023–24. That is not a current measurement of the protesting upper-secondary lycées. It does show that missing lessons were a problem before these demonstrations.

Funding shortages, recruitment difficulties and organisation can overlap. Calling it all waste avoids investigating those causes. Assuming a bigger budget will solve every problem sidesteps the same work.

A credible choice has two sides

The strongest objection to spending cuts is valid: they can damage services and weaken the economy. A financial target may then be met on paper while citizens receive less in return. Some bottlenecks genuinely require more staff or maintenance.

But necessary spending must still be funded. The government has to say which revenues it will raise, which other spending it will limit and where better organisation can actually help. Hoped-for efficiency savings cannot be treated as money already secured.

Our France debt page lets readers inspect the official observations. Their reference period matters: the moving counter is a model, not a measurement of the cost of these riots. Across the euro area, those figures help readers assess choices; they do not make those choices on voters’ behalf.

A teacher-replacement plan should deliver demonstrably more lessons. A tax measure should state who pays. A spending reduction should explain what will no longer be possible. Only then is a requested sacrifice connected to an outcome people can check, rather than another appeal for patience.

A window is repaired when new glass is fitted. The state’s credibility is restored only when its promises are still being kept after the budget vote.

Sources and methodology

This is opinion: judgments about fiscal credibility are distinguished from sourced facts. Researched, fully drafted, translated and checked with AI assistance; no independent human or native-language final review is claimed. The calculation assumes a new ten-year loan at the stated yield, issued at par, with unchanged principal and no fees. It does not measure France’s actual budget losses from unrest. The TEC10 index and an intraday benchmark yield are different observations. The Insee spending figure retains its publication vintage; the website’s Eurostat series may differ because of its publication date. The generated illustration does not document an actual event or damage following the unrest.
